dataset.name: Methane and CO2 chamber fluxes and porewater concentrations US-OWC Ameriflux wetland site, 2015-2018
description: The data measurements of CH4 and CO2 at different patch types (classified by dominant macrophyte vegetation or hydrological state). CH4 and CO2 data include 3 types of measurements: 1) Surface flux measurements from chamber measurements. 2) Leaf flux measurements from plant chambers, providing the rate per leaf area of methane flow through three species of macropyte aerenchemous plants (Water Lily, American Lotus, and Cattail) with the corresponding flux of CO2 at the same leaves. 3) Pore water concentrations of dissolved CO2 and CH4 concentrations. These are measured along vertical profiles at varying depths from the soil-water interface using in-situ porewater dialysis profiles (peepers). Observations of 1 and 3 are available monthly for most months of the growing season (May-September) of 2015, 2016 and 2018. Leaf flux measurements (plant chambers) are available only in June, July and August of 2018. We also included the patch type classification maps during 2015, 2017 and 2018 the relative water elevation map (bathymetry) for the site.

In 8/23/2020 we added the data file ChamberFluxes_2018_Separated_Diffusive_Ebullitive_Fluxes.xlsx with observation related to chamber measurements in OWC during September 2018. In these observations, we partitioned the methane flux to its diffusive and ebullitive components, using an analysis approach we describe in section 5 of the methods "Ebullition and diffusion partitioning".

measurementTechnique:
Porewater Dissolved Methane and CO2 Concentration Measurements: Peeper
Porewater samples for determining CO2 and CH4 concentrations were collected using in-situ dialysis samplers (peepers) described by MacDonald et al. (2013), following the procedure described in Angle et al. (2017). The peepers feature 20 stacked (61.4 ml) cells at a 2.8 cm vertical resolution. Each cell has a (22.5 cm2) windows covered with a 0.22 µm membrane that allows the water inside the cell to equilibrate with dissolved gas concentrations in the sediments. Cells were fitted with two sampling ports consisting of plastic tubing that allowed water extraction and refill. At each sampling, a 10 ml water sample was extracted from each cell through one tubing, while the other tubing remained connected to a container with N2 to avoid oxygen intrusion. After the sample extraction, the cell was refilled with deionized water degassed with N2. Samples were placed in 10 ml container pre-acidified with 0.2 ml HCl 2M, refrigerated and transported to the laboratory for further processing.
In the laboratory, dissolved CO2 and CH4 concentrations were determined using the Gas chromatography headspace equilibration technique described by (Kampbell et al., 1989). For samples collected in 2015 and 2016 we equilibrate subsamples of 5 ml of sampled water with a 20 ml N2 headspace, whereas for the samples collected in 2018, we equilibrated subsampled of 3 ml with a 57 ml N2 headspace. Upon equilibration, we injected 10 ml of headspace into 10-ml pre-evacuated vials and analyzed them in a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014, Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with a flame ionization detector fitted with a 1.8 Poropack Q column. We used Helium (25ml min-1) as the carrier gas for CO2 and methane analysis. We included CO2 and methane check standards every 20 samples to ensure that the chromatograph maintained the calibration throughout the analysis. If the deviation between the measured value and the value of the check standard was greater than 10%, we recalibrated the chromatograph and re-ran the samples.
We calculated CO2 and methane molar concentrations (mC) in the liquid phase, from the measured gas concentrations in the headspace as:
mC =(p_i/RT*Vh+p_i/H_i *Vl)/Vl (1)
Where p_i is the partial pressure of CO2 or methane (Headspace concentration (ppm) × ambient pressure at room conditions (0.010325 MPa)), R is the universal gas constant (0.008314 (L MPa K-1 mol-1), T is the room temperature (K), Vh is the volume of the headspace (ml), H_i is the Henry’s volatility constant for each gas (2.96 and 67.13 L Mpa mol-1, for CO2 and methane respectively), and Vl the volume of the liquid subsample used to create the headspace (ml).

Methane Flux from Chamber Measurements: Manual/Shimadzu
We used closed, non-steady state chambers to sample CO2 and methane along two transects covering 4 land cover types as described in Morin et al. (2017) and Rey-Sanchez et al. (2018). The chambers were made of transparent high-density polyethylene boxes with a surface area of 38 × 56 cm and a height of 26 cm. The bottom of the chamber was covered with a polyethylene pipe insulation at the bottom edge for flotation and seal with the water surface. The chambers were equipped with a thermometer to record temperatures inside the chamber during each deployment, a 3-m long Tygon tubing (1.6 mm internal diameter) for pressure relief and a 20 mm grey butyl stopper in the top that served as a sampling port. During each chamber deployment (20 min each), 7 gas samples were extracted every 5 minutes with a syringe and placed in 10 ml pre-evacuated vials. The vials were analyzed later in the laboratory with a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014, Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with a flame ionization detector fitted with a 1.8 Poropack Q column. We used Helium (25ml min-1) as the carrier gas for CO2 and methane analysis. We included CO2 and methane check standards every 20 samples to ensure that the chromatograph maintained the calibration throughout the analysis. If the deviation between the measured value and the value of the check standard was greater than 10%, we recalibrated the chromatograph and re-ran the samples.
Mass/volume concentrations of samples were calculated using a modified gas law, following the procedure described in Holland et al. (1999):
Cm= (Cv*P)/(R*T) (2)
where Cm is the mass/volume concentration of the gas (i.e. µmol CH4 L-1), Cv is the volume (ppm) of gas, P is atmospheric pressure (atm), R is the universal gas constant (0.0820575 L atm K-1mol-1), and T is the air temperature (K) of the chamber.
The accumulation rate (Crate) was determined using the slope of the linear regression fitted to the time points collected for each chamber. The flux rate (Fmanual, µmol CH4 m-2 s-1) was calculated as:
F_manual = (V*C_rate)/A (3)
where V is volume of chamber (m^3), C_rate is the accumulation rate in µmol CH4 m-3 s-1, and A is area of soil surface (m^2).

Methane Flux from Chamber Measurements: Picarro Gas Scouter
CO2 and methane fluxes were determined simultaneously by cavity ring-down spectroscopy using a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (Gas Scouter G4301, Picarro, Santa Clara, CA) coupled to custom made transparent polyethylene dome-shaped chambers. The chambers (842 cm^2 surface area, 11442 cm^3 volume) were equipped with a thermometer to record temperatures inside the chamber during deployment, and had a 12v fan for air mixing. The chambers recirculated at a flow rate of 1 L min-1, and recorded the CO2 and methane concentrations at a frequency of 1 Hz. Three replicates of chamber deployments were conducted consecutively at each peeper location.
In each chamber measurement, we fitted a 2 minute, 1 Hz time series of CO2 or methane concentrations, C_HM (µmol mol -1), to the non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981; Kutzbach et al., 2007; Pedersen et al., 2010):
C_HM=CS+ (C0- CS ) *e^(-kt) (4)
Where C0 is the pre-deployment concentration of methane or CO2 (µmol mol-1), Cs is the constant source or sink concentration (µmol mol-1), and k is a curve shape parameter (s-1). C0, Cs, and k are parameters determined by fitting the observed gas concentrations in the chamber over time, t (s). We then calculated the flux, F_Diff, of methane and CO2, (µmol m-2 s-1) at the wetland surface as:
F_Diff =k *(C0- CS)*pV/RTchA (5)
Where p (kPa) is the atmospheric pressure, measured at a nearby eddy covariance tower (Ameriflux site ID: US-OWC, Bohrer, 2018); V the volume of the chamber (m^3), R the universal gas constant (0.0083145 m^3 kPa mol-1 K-1), Tch the temperature inside the chamber (K), A the surface area enclosed in the chamber (m^2).

Patch-Type Maps
We include the georeferenced images (geotiff) of the wetland classified into patch types (matching the CMB_SPP variable in the Chamber data worksheet). Patch types were classified using k-means classification of google earth images from 2015 and 2017 (image dates are listed as the file name), combined with manual interpretation for the patch type value base don observation in the field, where 1 = open water, 2 = Typha, and 3 = Nelumbo. In 2015 and 2017 we did not discern Nymphaea from Nelumbo for patch classification, however there was very low abundance of water lily (Nymphaea). Mud flats were very small in 2015 and non-existing in 2017, and 2018. While some chamber in 2015, 2016 where measured in mud flat, we did not include a patch classified as mud flat in the maps. The 2018 map was made by manual modification of the 2017 map, based on observations in the field.
Water Elevation Map
We include the georeferenced images (geotiff) of the spatial variation of wetland water elevation (depth) relative to a fixed reference point. The actual water depth is temporally variable, and the water depth at the reference elevation for our site is available at National Estuarine Research
Reserve System Centralized Data Management Office (http://cdmo.baruch.sc.edu/get/landing.cfm ).
The wetland water elevation map was produce using a spline of field data measurements conducted using biosonics hydroacoustic system (BioSonics Inc, Seattle, WA), with additional manual depth measurements in shallow areas covered by cattails, and assuming depth = 0 for the water edge.

Ebullition and diffusion partitioning
We developed an approach to separate diffusive and ebullitive fluxes from each chamber deployment. We assume that diffusive fluxes are characterized by a relatively slow and consistent incremental increase of the methane concentration in the chamber while bubbling events are associated with intermittent rapid concentration increase. We used an empirical threshold to identify which timesteps at the high-frequency concentration time series were affected by bubbling. To determine the value of that threshold, we plotted methane concentration versus time, in each chamber deployment. We used the plots to visually identify the deployments that had an apparent monotonous increase and lacked any rapid concentration increase that may be associated with bubbling events. There were 12 chambers in total that met such a criterion, eight from open water patches and four from floating-leaved patches. We used these chambers to determine the maximum rate of change in CH_4 empirically that could be expected during measurements with diffusive flux only (Max_Diff, µmol mol^-1 s^-1):
Max_Diff=max ((∆CH_4)/∆t) ∀ chambers with only diffusive fluxes (1)
Where CH_4, is the methane concentration in µmol mol^-1, t is time in s, and ∆ marks a difference across a single high-frequency observation timestep. We found that Max_Diff = 0.058 µmol mol^-1 s^-1. Then, we assumed that increments larger than Max_Diff were caused by ebullition and used it as the condition to identify bubbling events in the rest of the chambers. We limited the analyses to the measured concentrations from chamber close until the maximum concentration observed in the chamber.
To calculate the ebullitive flux, we identify the times within the high frequency signal that correspond with bubbling events in the chamber methane concentration signal as,
t_i= {t_i∈{t_first:t_last } | {(∆CH_4)/∆t>Max_Diff }} (2)
defining i is an index for the timesteps affected by bubbles, out of the full time series of the chamber, tj, with j an index for observation timestep, running from the first timestep after the chamber was closed to the last timestep before the max concentration was reached. We calculate the episodic increase in methane concentration due to ebullition (Eb, µmol mol-1) as the change in methane concentrations occurred during the timesteps identified as affected by bubbles, ti.
Eb =∑_i(∆CH_4i) ∀ t_i (3)
We calculate the ebullitive flux (FCH4Eb, µmol m-2 s-1) for each chamber as:
FCH_4Eb =Eb/((t_last-t_first ) )(P V)/(R T A) (4)
Where P is the atmospheric pressure (Pa), V is the chamber volume (m^3), R is the universal gas constant (m^3 Pa K^-1 mol^-1), T is the temperature in the chamber (C), and A is the surface area of the chamber (m^2).
We transform the observed time series of methane concentration, CH_4 to a corresponding time series that excludes the effects of bubbles, CH’_4. We exclude all points identified as directly affected by bubbling events at timesteps ti. Then we subtract the concentration increment that was added to the chamber during these times, prior to any remaining observation, to obtain CH’4 (see illustration in Fig 2.B):
CH'_4j =CH_4j - ∑_(i
We fitted this transformed “diffusive only” concentration timeseries, CH’_4 to the non-linear Hutchinson and Mosier one-dimension diffusion model (Hutchinson and Mosier, 1981; Kutzbach et al., 2007; Pedersen et al., 2010).
CH'_4≈C_HM=C_(s ) + (C_0- C_(s ) )e^(-kt) (6)
Where C_HM, (µmol mol^-1) is the modelled time series of methane concentration in the chamber, C0 represents the pre-deployment concentration of methane (µmol mol^-1), Cs is the constant source or sink concentration (µmol mol^-1), and k is a curve shape parameter (s^-1). C_0, C_(s ), and k are parameters determined by fitting the observed segment-gas concentrations in the chamber over time, t (s). We used the coefficient of determination (r^2) of the fit between the non-linear model and concentration observations inside the chambers as quality control for the observation. Chamber observations with r^2 < 0.8 were deemed of poor quality and were omitted from estimates of the relative contribution to the net surface flux. We then calculate the diffusive flux of methane at the water surface (CH_4Diff, µmol m^-2 s^-1) as:
FCH_4Diff =k(C_0- C_(s ) )(P V )/(R T A) (7)
We used the coefficient of determination (r^2) of the fit between the non-linear model and concentration observations inside the chambers. Flux measurements with r^2 < 0.8 were deemed of poor quality and were omitted from estimates of the relative contribution to the net surface flux and comparisons of diffusive fluxes made between patches. Our rationale here was that even though our method did not allow the identification of a diffusive flux signal, we could not rule out that diffusion was taking place. We calculate the net flux from the water surface, FCH_4Net, as:
FCH_(4Net )= FCH_4Eb+ FCH_4Diff (8)

Methods for Methane and CO2 fluxes through plants – Data file “PlantChambersFlux_2018”. This file was added to teh data packadge on 11/12/2022
The goals and results of the plant fluxes measurements, including a more detailed account of the methods is listed in [Villa et al., 2020] https://doi.org/10.1002/lno.11467.
Data collection methods:
Methane flux and CO2 uptake were determined simultaneously by cavity ring-down spectroscopy, using a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (Picarro G4301, Santa Clara, CA) coupled to custom-made leaf chambers. Chambers consisted of transparent plastic storage boxes sealed with rimmed weather stripping and large binder clips. Chambers were fitted with a digital thermometer to monitor and record the temperature inside the chamber. Previous experiments on leaf chambers under sunny conditions indicate that while net photosynthesis is not affected by the time of enclosure despite a significant increase in temperature, changes can occur in methane fluxes and stomatal conductance after 8 minutes of chamber deployment [Knapp and Yavitt, 1992]. To avoid such effects on stomatal conductance, we deployed our chambers for a conservative total measurement time of 4 minutes during which the chamber is closed. The Gas Scouter recirculates the air within the chamber while monitoring CO2 and CH4 concentrations simultaneously at a frequency of 1 Hz. The flow rate of chamber air through the Gas Scouter is ~1 L min-1. The chamber used for sampling cattails had a volume of 3.364 L, and enclosed a section of few leaves, while the volume of the chamber used for American lotuses and water lilies was bigger (12.437 L) allowing for the accommodation of an entire leaf without disruption. In addition, the chamber for floating-leaved species had two floating foams attached outside the chamber that kept it raised above the water level. Samplings were conducted monthly, from June through August 2018.
The sampling period encompassed the macrophyte peak growing season at OWC, aiming to exclude spring and fall transitions of vegetation growth and senescence that could bias the flux measurements. Sampling was conducted in the central portion of the estuary. Every month, we randomly selected 5 adjacent leaves (floating-leaved species, Nelumbo, Nymphaea) or leaf sections (cattail, Typha) at different locations. At each monthly sampling, chambers were deployed at three parts of the day: morning (8:00 to 11:00), midday (13:00 to 15:00) and afternoon (14:00 to 20:00). The morning time period included the peak in methane emissions (around 8:30 am), previously identified by Rey-Sánchez et al. [2018] in the sampling site. During each monthly campaign, we conducted the sampling of one species during a single day, except for June, when we sampled American lotus and water lily at the same day and cattail at the next day.
Chambers were placed on the same leaves during the morning, midday and afternoon of the same day. These leaves were harvested at the end of the day. Chambers in cattails were placed 50 cm above the water surface, which was within the upper 2/3 of the leaves and included 5 replicates of 4 – 6 leaf sections arrays at each enclosure. The sheath of the cattail leaves that we sampled was below the water level in all samplings. Measurements in American lotuses and water lilies were conducted on single floating leaves at 5 replicates as well. The leaves we sampled were already directly exposed to the atmosphere (i.e., not submerged). For gas flux measurements, the leaves were raised from the water surface and isolated in the chamber. After the sampling we checked for visible mechanical damage to the leaves that may have been caused during the daily sampling and thus compromised the sampling. We did not have to replace any measurement due to damage to leaves.
We measured the one-sided leaf area directly enclosed by the chamber by harvesting the leaves we sampled. We used one-sided leaf area because in the floating-leaf species methane flux to the air is done through the upper side of the leaf that is exposed to the air. Furthermore, one-sided leaf area is the standard vegetation property observed from remote sensing. To scale the flux from per leaf area in the chamber to flux per ground area for the plant type we also estimated the general leaf area index (LAI, m2 m-2) of each species after each diurnal sampling using a 0.25 m2 PVC frame (5 replicates) in the immediate area where we sampled. For American lotuses and water lilies, we took digital photographs that were processed to measure the proportion of area covered by leaves and then normalized by the area of the frame. We did not account for overlapping leaf areas as we assumed that submerged covered leaves do not participate actively in the exchange of gases with the atmosphere. Accordingly, the possible maximum LAI measured in floating-leaved species was 1. For cattails, we harvested the leaves inside the frame, clipping them at the water surface level, bagged and transported the leaves to the laboratory for further processing. Leaves from the June sampling were carefully measured to determine the area, then dried and weighted to generate an empirical allometric equation of specific leaf area to estimate LAI (unitless, m2 leaf/m2 ground) as a function of dry weight, W, (g) (LAI = 51W/Af + 12.1, r2 = 0.93, p < 0.001, where Af is the sample frame area, 0.25 m2). We used this function to approximate the cattail LAI for July and August as a function of the dry weight of harvested biomass samples. We assumed that this allometric relationship between LAI and dry weight did not significantly change during the peak growing season.
In each chamber measurement, we fitted the 4 minute, 1 Hz time series of methane or CO2 concentrations, C_HM (µmol mol -1), to the non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model [Hutchinson and Mosier, 1981; Kutzbach et al., 2007; Pedersen et al., 2010]:
C_HM=C_(s )+ (C_0- C_(s ) ) e^(-kt) (1)
Where C0 is the pre-deployment concentration of methane or CO2 (µmol mol-1), Cs is the constant source or sink concentration (µmol mol-1), and k is a curve shape parameter (s-1). C0, Cs, and k are determined by fitting the observed gas concentrations in the chamber over time, t (s), to eq. 1. We then calculated the flux, F, of methane and CO2, FCH4 and FCO2, respectively, (µmol mleaf-2 s-1) at the leaf surface as:
F=k (C_0- C_(s ) ) (p V)/(R Tch A) (2)
Where p (Pa) is the atmospheric pressure, measured at a nearby eddy covariance tower (Ameriflux site ID: US-OWC, [Bohrer 2016-] doi:10.17190/AMF/1418679); V the volume of the chamber (m3), R the universal gas constant (8.314 m3 Pa mol-1 K-1), Tch the temperature inside the chamber (K) and A the area of the leaf enclosed in the chamber (m2).
Examples for our flux calculation approach and quality control are provided in Figure S2. Out of the 135 flux measurements, we discarded 31 where the goodness of fit for CHM was lower than 0.9 (r2 < 0.9) in either methane flux or CO2 uptake. Discarded data were evenly distributed among species and did not show discernible patterns with the times of the day or month of sampling, except for measurements of cattails in June during morning time, which were all discarded.
